statement: A rule holds one fact: one default or one behaviour, as it holds today. An ADR section with several facts becomes several rules, linked through `related`.

events.why: A card that holds a paragraph brings back the problem of digging a default out of an ADR.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: A rule has an `id`, a `statement`, a `status` and `events`. It may also have `experimental`, `repo`, `values`, `knob`, `errors`, `code`, `since`, `target`, `related`, `supersededBy` and `aliases`.

events.why: Each field answers one question a reader asks about a fact: its value, how to change it, where it's built, since when.
Rules about the repo need a flag, since they never ship in a version.
events.prev: A rule has an `id`, a `statement`, a `status` and `events`. It may also have `experimental`, `values`, `knob`, `errors`, `code`, `since`, `target`, `related`, `supersededBy` and `aliases`.

events.why: In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: A statement is one or two sentences in the present tense that say what holds, with no why. It follows `docs/writing.md`.

events.why: A card should read as a fact; the why changes over time and lives in the events.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: A rule's current why is the `why` of its newest `decided`, `amended` or `clarified` event. There's no separate field for it.

events.why: A separate field would drift from the history it summarises.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: A rule id is `<prefix>.<slug>` in kebab-case and never changes. A renamed or moved rule gets a new id and keeps the old one in `aliases`.

events.why: ADRs cite ids, and aliases keep those links working.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: A rule that stops holding changes status. It's never deleted.

events.why: The history of a fact that no longer holds is still the answer to why it changed.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: A rule's status is one of six: `active`, `decided`, `proposed`, `withdrawn`, `rejected` or `superseded`. Merged but unreleased work is a `built` event, not a status, except that a repo rule is `active` from its `built` event.

events.why: Status answers whether the rule holds today; events say what happened.
A repo rule is in force once its PR merges.
events.prev: A rule's status is one of six: `active`, `decided`, `proposed`, `withdrawn`, `rejected` or `superseded`. Merged but unreleased work is a `built` event, not a status.

events.why: In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: An alternative becomes a `rejected` rule only when it answers a real "why don't you just…?" question, and its `why` names that question.

events.why: A board full of rejections would bury the rules that hold.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: An event has a `type`, a `date`, a `ref` and a one-line `why`. The type is one of twelve: `proposed`, `decided`, `clarified`, `amended`, `built`, `shipped`, `corrected`, `reopened`, `removed`, `rejected`, `withdrawn` and `superseded`.

events.why: These are the steps a decision went through while the ADRs were grilled.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: A `clarified` or `amended` event carries `prev`, the wording or behaviour before it.

events.why: The rule as it was can then be read without opening the ADR.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: An event's `ref` is something a reader can open on GitHub: `adr/NNNN#anchor` for an ADR heading (the anchor is required), `#N` or `repo#N` for a PR or an issue, or `vX.Y.Z` for a release tag. Each event type takes only the ref kinds in decision 6's table, and grilling notes and agent memory are never a source.

events.why: A reader has to be able to check every event.
A ref opens at the decision it means.
events.prev: An event's `ref` is something a reader can open on GitHub: an ADR section, a PR, an issue or a release tag. Grilling notes and agent memory are never a source.

events.why: In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: Concepts are a fixed list in `docs/rules/concepts.json`, each with an id, a prefix, a name, a description and an order. Each rule belongs to exactly one concept.

events.why: One concept per rule keeps the board from showing a rule twice; cross-links go through `related`.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: The registry is JSON, one file per concept in `docs/rules/`, validated by `scripts/rules/check.ts` with no library. `schema.json` gives editors hints only.

events.why: One file per concept keeps a PR's diff inside the concept it touches, and the repo owns its checks.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: The registry is the source of truth for what holds today. ADRs keep the story of why.

events.why: A fact often has several ADRs behind it and fields no ADR has, so it can't live inside one ADR.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: Each decision and each amendment in an ADR ends with a `Rules:` line naming the rules it adds or changes.

events.why: The line ties an ADR to its rules, and the checks read it.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: `pnpm rules:check` runs in CI. It fails on a malformed registry, an unknown or repeated id, a broken ADR ref, a status that doesn't match its fields and events, a repo rule with a version or a shipped event, a missing `code` path or an out-of-date README.

events.why: Each of these is a way the registry could quietly be wrong.
Repo rules have their own fields and events to check.
events.prev: `pnpm rules:check` runs in CI. It fails on a malformed registry, an unknown or repeated id, a broken ADR ref, a status that doesn't match its fields and events, a missing `code` path or an out-of-date README.

events.why: In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: A PR that changes an ADR with `Rules:` lines, or any ADR from 0026 on, also changes `docs/rules/`, unless it's labelled `no-rules`.

events.why: A fact must change in the same PR as the ADR that changes it.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: A PR fails if a rule id or alias on `main` is missing from it. The `no-rules` label doesn't skip this.

events.why: Rules are never deleted, and links from ADRs must keep working.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: Every decision and amendment in an ADR numbered 0026 or higher has a `Rules:` line from the start. Older ADRs are checked once they have `Rules:` lines.

events.why: New ADRs shouldn't add to the backfill.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: Whoever changes an ADR updates its rules in the same PR. The steward treats rules that don't match the ADR as a must-fix.

events.why: CI catches a registry left untouched; only a review catches one that says the wrong thing.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: `pnpm rules:ship <version>` runs in the version PR. Each rule whose `target` is that version becomes `active`, with `since` set, a `shipped` event and no `target`.

events.why: Shipped events are generated, so a card's version can't be wrong.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: `pnpm rules:build` writes `docs/rules/README.md`, which is committed: per concept, a table of rules, then each rule's history.

events.why: Agents and GitHub readers get every fact and every why in one file, with no tooling.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: `pnpm rules:board` writes one self-contained page with the registry inlined to `.rules-board/index.html`, which is gitignored, and opens it. It has the Board, a rule drawer and the Agenda by day or by version.

events.why: The board is the view for reading across concepts and over time.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: Rules for the existing ADRs are added one concept per PR, each reviewed by the maintainer. Supervision, Durability and Versioning & releases go first.

events.why: Each PR stays small enough to check against its ADRs.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: `AGENTS.md` sends agents to `docs/rules/README.md` for what holds today.

events.why: Agents can't find the registry from the file tree alone.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: The registry covers this repo's ADRs only.

events.why: CI can only hold this repo's ADR PRs to their rules.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: The rules registry is internal tooling outside the milestones, and its PRs take the `no-changeset` label.

events.why: It ships nothing to npm and waits for no release.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: `rules:check` fails when a `decided` or `proposed` rule's `target` is at or below the packages' version. Previews such as `0.2.0-next.3` never trigger it.

events.why: The version PR that sets a version is where its rules ship.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: A patch from a `release/0.x` branch gets its `shipped` events in that branch's version PR, and they come to `main` with the backport.

events.why: The branch is where the patch's version is set.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: A rule with `repo: true` is about how this repo works, not the published packages. It's `active` from its `built` event, has no `since`, `target` or `shipped` event, and `rules:ship` skips it.

events.why: Repo tooling and process never ship in an npm version, but they are in force once merged.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: Under an ADR's `## Decision`, a decision is a numbered `###` heading when there are any, otherwise a top-level numbered item, otherwise each `###` section. A heading that says "amended" is an amendment, and a `Rules:` line inside a code fence doesn't count.

events.why: The `Rules:` line check has to know which parts of an ADR need a line.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: On a docs-only pull request, `check` runs in full and `cli-node24`, `browser`, `e2e` and `bench` report success without running their steps.

events.why: A docs change can't break runtime code, and the e2e and bench runs cost runner time for files they never read.
In force from the PR that built the docs-only skip and the nightly.

statement: A pull request is docs-only when every changed file is under `docs/`, `.changeset/` or `.claude/`, or ends in `.md`. Any other file makes it a full run.

events.why: An allowlist defaults to the full run, so a kind of file nobody listed never skips the tests.
In force from the PR that built the docs-only skip and the nightly.

statement: On a docs-only pull request the `e2e` jobs run and skip their steps, so `e2e (chromium)`, `e2e (firefox)` and `e2e (webkit)` still report as required checks.

events.why: A matrix job skipped as a whole reports one unexpanded `e2e` check, and the required names would stay pending.
In force from the PR that built the docs-only skip and the nightly.

statement: Only `pull_request` runs can be docs-only. Release dry runs and stage runs, the nightly, pushes and runs by hand always run every job they include.

events.why: A release run is the last full check before npm, so it must never skip.
In force from the PR that built the docs-only skip and the nightly.

statement: Every CI job, `bench` included, runs on `main` each night at 03:00 UTC, through `nightly.yml` calling `ci.yml`.

events.why: With docs-only PRs skipping e2e, a daily full run catches flaky tests, browser drift and interactions between PRs merged the same day; it replaces the weekly run.
In force from the PR that built the docs-only skip and the nightly.

statement: A scheduled nightly is skipped when `main` has no commits since the last green nightly. A nightly run by hand always runs.

events.why: A night with nothing new can only repeat the last result.
In force from the PR that built the docs-only skip and the nightly.

statement: A failed nightly opens an issue labelled `nightly-failure`, or comments on the open one, with the failed jobs and the commits since the last green nightly. The next green nightly closes it.

events.why: GitHub emails a failed scheduled run only to whoever last edited the workflow; an issue is seen by everyone, and the commit range points at the cause.
In force from the PR that built the docs-only skip and the nightly.

statement: We don't use `paths-ignore` or a path-filter action to skip CI for docs.

events.why: Why not just `paths-ignore`? The workflow wouldn't start, so the required checks would stay pending and the PR couldn't merge; a path-filter action is a dependency for a dozen lines of shell.

statement: The repo is a pnpm 12 workspace, run with plain `pnpm -r` in dependency order and no task runner on top.

events.why: A workspace and dependency order cover what this repo needs.
The workspace skeleton.

statement: Development and CI run on Node 26 LTS, pinned in `.nvmrc`.

events.why: One Node version for every contributor and every CI job.
The workspace skeleton.

statement: Type checking runs `tsc --noEmit` from TypeScript 7 in every package, and editors, the checker and tsgolint use the same version.

events.why: One TypeScript version, so the checker, the editor and lint never disagree.
The workspace skeleton.

statement: Lint is oxlint with `oxlint-tsgolint`, type-aware on every run, and formatting is oxfmt.

events.why: Fast enough to run on every save, and from the same project as the bundler.
Lint, format and dependency rules.

statement: The repo doesn't use ESLint, typescript-eslint or Prettier.

events.why: Why not the usual ESLint and Prettier? They're much slower, and typescript-eslint's type-aware rules need TypeScript's JS API, which TypeScript 7 doesn't offer as stable yet.

statement: Packages are built with tsdown, which writes the `.d.ts` files through `isolatedDeclarations` with no type checker in the build. Apps and the dev server use Vite 8.

events.why: tsdown runs on the same Rolldown core as Vite, and doesn't need TypeScript's JS API.
The workspace skeleton.

statement: Unit and browser tests run on Vitest 5, as projects in the root config. End-to-end tests and the browser benches run on Playwright in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit.

events.why: One test runner for Node and the browser, and a real browser for each engine.
The workspace skeleton.

statement: Tools are only called through root scripts (`pnpm format`, `lint`, `typecheck`, `test`, `build`, `e2e`, `check`), never as a tool binary. `pnpm check` runs the format check, lint, typecheck and unit tests.

events.why: Swapping a tool means editing one script, and CI shows the swap changed nothing.
The workspace skeleton.

statement: The repo has no git hooks. CI is the only gate.

events.why: Hooks are one more dependency, slow every commit, and `--no-verify` skips them anyway.
The workspace skeleton.

statement: Every published package compiles with `isolatedDeclarations: true`, so every export has an explicit type. Private packages and the CLI, which publishes no `.d.ts`, keep normal inference.

events.why: A body change can then never change the published `.d.ts` without a visible diff.
The workspace skeleton.

statement: Imports between packages resolve to source through the `@isoloop/source` export condition, so type checking, lint and tests need no build first. `publishConfig.exports` replaces it on publish.

events.why: Building first makes every check wait for a build and points errors at `dist`.
The workspace skeleton.

statement: A package can only import what its `package.json` lists (pnpm's strict `node_modules`), oxlint `no-restricted-imports` sets the allowed imports per package, and `bus` compiles with no DOM types.

events.why: The package boundaries are checked by tools rather than by review.
Lint, format and dependency rules.

statement: Every lint rule is an error or off; there are no warnings. The `correctness`, `suspicious` and `perf` groups and the type-aware TypeScript rules are errors, and other rules are added by name.

events.why: Warnings pile up unread, and promise rules matter in a message-passing runtime.
Lint, format and dependency rules.

statement: oxfmt uses single quotes, semicolons, a print width of 100 and trailing commas everywhere, with defaults otherwise.

events.why: It matches the code samples in the design docs.
Lint, format and dependency rules.

statement: Isoloop supports Baseline "widely available" browsers, and the packages build to `es2022`. The minimums for the features it relies on are Chrome 108, Firefox 114 and Safari 16.4.

events.why: Features in every major engine for 30 months or more cover what the runtime needs.
The minimums were looked up per feature in MDN's browser-compat-data.
events.prev: Baseline "widely available", with no version numbers named.

events.why: First released in 0.1.0.

statement: `createKernel` checks for module workers, `MessageChannel`, adopted stylesheets and OPFS, and throws `unsupported_browser` naming whatever is missing.

events.why: A missing feature fails at start with its name, not later with a confusing error.
The browser feature check.
First released in 0.1.0.

statement: Every tool version is pinned exactly, with no `^`, in the pnpm `catalog:` in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`.

events.why: Caret ranges let 0.x tools change behaviour without a PR.
The workspace skeleton.

statement: Dependabot opens one grouped PR a week for npm and GitHub Actions minors and patches, with a 3-day cooldown. Majors come as separate PRs.

events.why: Dependabot is built into GitHub, where Renovate is one more app to install.
CI, Dependabot and Pages.

statement: pnpm refuses versions younger than 3 days (`minimumReleaseAge: 4320`), lifecycle scripts stay blocked unless allow-listed by name, peers are strict, and GitHub Actions are pinned by commit SHA.

events.why: A compromised release is usually caught within days, and install scripts are the usual way in.
The workspace skeleton.

statement: `packageManager: "pnpm@12.16.1"` pins pnpm. Contributors install pnpm's standalone binary, and corepack isn't used.

events.why: One field pins the version for contributors and for CI's `pnpm/action-setup`.
The workspace skeleton.

statement: VS Code settings are committed in `.vscode/`: the workspace TypeScript, oxc as the formatter, format on save and oxlint diagnostics.

events.why: Editors then use the same tools and versions as CI.
Lint, format and dependency rules.

statement: CI runs on Ubuntu only. The `browser`, `e2e` and `bench` jobs start only after `check` passes, and install browsers through one local action with time limits, retries and caches.

events.why: One OS keeps CI fast, and the browser jobs skip a run that already failed its checks.
CI, Dependabot and Pages.
Time-limited, retried Playwright install with a browser cache.

statement: The repo uses no NX, turbo or Vite+ task graph.

events.why: Why not cache builds with a task runner? It pays off in big monorepos; here it would mostly add config. It comes back if CI time becomes a problem.

statement: The top of a package's `src/` holds only its entries, the files `exports`, `bin` or the build point at, and tests named after them. dom keeps its entries in its four folders.

events.why: Entries are the files other things depend on by path, so they stay put and are easy to find.
The last packages moved, and the layout test's pending list went.

statement: Everything else in `src/` lives in an area: one level of kebab-case folders named for a concept from the system design, never for a kind (`utils`, `helpers`, `lib`, `common`, `misc`, `types`).

events.why: A folder named for a concept says where a change goes; one named for a kind collects anything.
The last packages moved into areas.

statement: `index.ts` is only ever an entry, a module imports the file that defines what it needs, and entries list what they export instead of `export *`.

events.why: Barrels hide where code lives and make import cycles easy.
protocol's and bus's entries name what they export.

statement: A test sits next to the code it tests. Files tests load by URL live in `src/__fixtures__/`, and helpers tests import live in `test/` at the package root, which holds no test files.

events.why: A test next to its code moves with it, and a fixture loaded by URL needs one known place.
The last packages moved.

statement: Shipped code never uses a relative path to leave its package; it imports other packages by name. Tests and fixtures may, to start another package's worker.

events.why: A relative import across packages skips the dependency rules and breaks once published.
The layout checks.

statement: A file that moves keeps its name, and a move changes nothing in `dist` except tsdown's source-path comments.

events.why: tsdown names shared declaration chunks after their first module, and the API check reads those names.
In force from the ADR's PR.

statement: History docs (ADRs, plans, posts, investigations) keep the paths of their day, living docs follow the code, and no living doc carries a folder map.

events.why: A folder map would drift, and the tree shows the layout anyway.
In force from the ADR's PR.

statement: Packages ship ESM only, one bundled file per entry plus tsdown's shared chunks.

events.why: One file per entry keeps what an app imports small and predictable.
First released in 0.1.0.

statement: Every package declares `sideEffects: false` except for its scripts (bus's worker, runtime's bootstrap and worker, the devtools panel), which are listed by both their `./src/` and `./dist/` paths.

events.why: Bundlers drop unused exports, and the files that run on load are named so they're kept.
The bundle guard, and scripts declared in `sideEffects`.
First released in 0.1.0.

statement: `bench/bundle-size` budgets each library entry's import-time code, seven app bundles and the four scripts, bundled with Vite's own `build()`. Each budget is its size at acceptance plus 5%, rounded up to the next 0.5 KB; a PR that crosses one raises it and says why.

events.why: A new global side effect or a heavier entry shows up as a number in CI.
The bundle guard, with budgets.

statement: oxlint fails `export *` barrels, import cycles and file names that aren't kebab-case, through `oxc/no-barrel-file`, `import/no-cycle` and `unicorn/filename-case`.

events.why: Three rules added by name, as the lint rules allow.
The layout checks, `import/no-cycle` and kebab-case file names.

statement: The layout test in `scripts/layout/`, run by `pnpm test`, checks the file tree: entries at the top, `index.ts` only as an entry, areas one level deep, fixtures and `test/` in their places, no relative escapes, every test in a Vitest project and every `./src/` `sideEffects` path existing.

events.why: There's no custom lint rule, since oxlint's JS plugins are alpha, so a test checks the tree.
The layout checks.

statement: `runtime` may import only `@isoloop/dom/worker`, `host` only `@isoloop/dom/host` and only in `render/isoloop-dom.ts`, `protocol`, `bus` and `codec` never import `dom`, and `dom` imports no other `@isoloop/*` package.

events.why: Each side of the render bridge sees only its own half, so a host-only API can't leak into a worker.
`@isoloop/dom`, the render bridge `isoloop-dom@1`.

statement: `dom`'s four source folders (`shared`, `worker`, `host`, `testing`) are each type-checked with their own tsconfig and `lib`. `worker` and `host` import `shared` but not each other.

events.why: A stray `document` in the worker half then fails the build, not a review.
`@isoloop/dom`, the render bridge `isoloop-dom@1`.

statement: The rules page has six tabs, routed by the URL's hash: Board, Agenda, Hive, Keywords, Timeline and Sources.

events.why: The prototypes showed each question needs its own view: what holds, what changed, what connects, which ideas cut across, when, and where from.

statement: The Hive tab draws one axis per concept and a dot per rule, ordered by first event date and coloured by status, with links as curves between axes.

events.why: It shows which concepts connect, and exploring one rule's links by hover reads well.

statement: The Keywords tab holds the keyword glossary, each keyword with its definition and its rules by concept, and the keyword map, which joins keywords that tag the same rules.

events.why: Keywords group ideas that cut across concepts, and the map shows how those ideas cluster.

statement: The Timeline tab shows every event in one lane per concept, by date, with release tags as lines, and a Churn heatmap counts `amended`, `clarified` and `corrected` events per concept and day.

events.why: It shows when decisions were made and where they keep changing.

statement: The Sources tab shows which ADRs feed which concepts, a treemap of the `code` paths rules cite, and a Health list of where the registry is weak.

events.why: It shows where facts come from, where they live in the code, and what the registry is missing.

statement: Board, Agenda and Hive have an "as of" option that rebuilds each rule as it stood on a chosen date or release, and a diff that lists what changed between two points.

events.why: Seeing what held at a release, and what changed since, answers what a release changed in facts rather than commits.

statement: "As of" places a whole day at once, since events have no time; earlier wording comes from `prev`, which is free text; only the statement and the status have a history.

events.why: Accepted for now: storing times and every field's earlier value is left for later.

statement: Links between rules are derived when the page is built, in four kinds: `related` and `supersededBy`, the same ADR section, a shared symbol, and a shared `code` path.

events.why: Written `related` links never cross concepts, so the links between concepts come from what rules already share.

statement: A key shared by more than 12 rules makes no links; the page lists it instead.

events.why: Without a cap, a file such as the kernel's links almost every rule to every other.

statement: A link from a key shared by n rules weighs 1/(n−1), so a narrow key counts more than a broad one.

events.why: Broad keys still connect rules, but a pair that shares a rare key is the stronger tie.

statement: Keywords are a fixed vocabulary in `docs/rules/keywords.json`, each with an id, a label, a one-line definition and aliases. A rule names its keywords in an optional `keywords` field, and `rules:check` fails on an unknown one.

events.why: Free tags drift; a vocabulary with definitions doubles as a glossary.

statement: The maintainer reviews the keywords on each concept's rules, one concept per PR.

events.why: Keywords tagged in bulk by a script over-matched common words; narrow keywords need judgement to place.

statement: Symbols are derived from backticked names in statements, knobs and errors, feed search and the shared-symbol links, and are never written by hand.

events.why: With hundreds of names, symbols work as search, not as filters.

statement: One config file holds what's particular to a repo: the title, the rules and ADR folders, the ADR number from which `Rules:` lines are required, the GitHub owner and repo for links, and where the page is written.

events.why: The scripts hold nothing about Isoloop, so the tooling can move to another repo unchanged.

statement: Each tab is its own module next to a small shell that holds the tabs, the shared filters, the theme and the rule drawer, and `rules:board` inlines them into one self-contained page.

events.why: Views are built and changed one at a time without touching the others.

statement: The rules tooling is a product-neutral tool with its own design system; nothing in its code, tokens or components is about Isoloop, and Isoloop uses it only as dev tooling.

events.why: It's meant to work for any repo's ADRs, so Isoloop is one user of it, not its subject.

statement: The rules tooling moves to a repo of its own later, and Isoloop's published packages never depend on it.

events.why: It's dev tooling for the repo; nothing a user installs should pull it in.

statement: Isoloop's palette is one theme, chosen in `rules.config.json`; a theme sets only the semantic tokens and may bring a webfont.

events.why: Keeping the product's own look separate from Isoloop's lets another repo pick its own theme.

statement: Design tokens come in three layers: primitives, semantic tokens and component tokens. Components read only semantic and component tokens, and themes change only the semantic layer.

events.why: One place per kind of decision: raw values, what a value is for, and what one component uses.

statement: Charts have 8 categorical colour slots, and a chart with more than 8 categories groups the rest.

events.why: More than 8 colours can't be told apart reliably.

statement: `rules:check` fails on a colour, a font size, a font family or a spacing value written in a component or a view, outside the files on one allowlist.

events.why: Literals in components are how a design system drifts.

statement: Components are plain functions that return HTML through an `html` tagged template, which escapes every value; `raw()` marks HTML that's already safe. There's no framework.

events.why: Escaping by default closes the injection holes string building leaves, with no dependency.

statement: Layout uses four primitives, Stack, Cluster, Grid and Split, spaced with `gap`; a component never sets its own outer margin.

events.why: Spacing belongs to the parent, so components fit anywhere without margin fights.

statement: Type has a 5-step scale (xs, s, m, l, xl) with tabular numbers where digits line up; data views stay at the m step or below. The default font is the system stack, and a theme may swap in a webfont.

events.why: Dense data reads better small and aligned, and a system font needs no download.

statement: Charts share one toolkit: scales, axes, a legend, a tooltip and SVG helpers.

events.why: Each view drawing its own axes would look and behave differently.

statement: CSS uses `@layer` (reset, tokens, base, layout, components, views), each class is prefixed with its owner, a component or a view, and there are no utility classes.

events.why: Layers settle precedence without specificity fights, and owner prefixes show where a style comes from.

statement: Until the product has a name, tokens use the placeholder prefix `--rb-` and classes `.rb-`, set in one place so a rename is one mechanical pass.

events.why: The name is still being chosen.

statement: `rules:board --specimen` writes a page with every token, type step, layout primitive, component and chart part.

events.why: One page to review the design system without opening every view.

statement: The design system is tested for WCAG AA contrast in both themes, for the literal ban, with unit tests per component, and with a headless smoke test of every view and the specimen at 2 widths in both themes; there are no pixel snapshots.

events.why: These catch what breaks in practice (unreadable colours, drift, broken markup, overflow, errors) without snapshots that fail on every intended change.
